channel.title: Film Theory
channel.description: Daily lessons from a 52-week film theory program

item.title: Week 6 · Day 5: Arnheim and “The Complete Film”: a defense of art against the sound film
item.description: For Arnheim, technology’s race to make film exactly like reality (sound, color, depth) is not progress but art losing its own material; a film that is a “complete” copy of reality is a film with nothing left to transform.

item.title: Week 6 · Day 4: Arnheim and “Film and Reality”: art born from defects
item.description: For Rudolf Arnheim, film can be an art not because it copies reality perfectly but, on the contrary, because it copies it incompletely and differently; the camera’s “defects” are the artist’s material.

item.title: Week 6 · Day 3: Münsterberg: memory, imagination, and the emotions
item.description: For Münsterberg, film is an art that overcomes the forms of the outer world (space, time, causality) and arranges events according to the forms of the inner world (attention, memory, imagination, emotion); the logic we saw yesterday in the close-up extends today to remembering, imagining, and feeling.

item.title: Week 6 · Day 2: Münsterberg and attention: the close-up as the mind made visible
item.description: For Münsterberg, film is not a record of the outer world but a world rearranged according to the workings of the spectator’s mind; the close-up is the clearest example of that rearrangement: it turns the mind’s act of attention into a concrete image on the screen.

item.title: Week 6 · Day 1: Silent-era film theory and the debate over the “essence of cinema”
item.description: To prove that cinema—then dismissed as fairground entertainment—was an art, the first silent-era theorists went looking for “what only cinema can do”; that search gave us concepts we still use today, but also the danger of locking cinema into a narrow definition of its “essence.”

item.title: Week 5 · Day 7: Test — What is film theory? Draw the map
item.description: This week you moved from looking at cinema to thinking about cinema; you saw three different maps: Stam’s historical map, Andrew’s four-question map and Elsaesser and Hagener’s map of the body; today we test whether you can read them.

item.title: Week 5 · Day 6: Film day — Sherlock Jr. (Buster Keaton, 1924)
item.description: Sherlock Jr. stages the question you read about this week — “what is film theory?” — as a forty-five-minute comedy: is the screen a window, a door, or a mirror?

item.title: Week 5 · Day 5: Mirror, eye, skin, ear, brain — the distance closes
item.description: In the second half of Elsaesser and Hagener’s sequence of metaphors, the screen first becomes a mirror that shows spectators themselves, then an eye, a field of exchanged looks; finally the film enters the skin, the ear and the brain — that is, the inside of the body — and the distance between spectator and screen almost entirely closes.

item.title: Week 5 · Day 4: Thinking cinema through the body — window, frame, door
item.description: For Elsaesser and Hagener, every film theory, implicitly or explicitly, is a model of the relationship between the spectator’s body and the screen; this relationship begins with looking from a distance (window, frame) and moves toward stepping inside the screen (door).

item.title: Week 5 · Day 3: Dudley Andrew and the four questions of theory
item.description: According to Dudley Andrew, every film theory, whether it says so openly or not, answers the same four questions: what is cinema’s raw material, by what methods is this material worked, what forms result, and what is the purpose or value of it all?

item.title: Week 5 · Day 2: The “prehistory” of film theory (part 2) — thinking about cinema before cinema
item.description: Film theory did not start from scratch in 1895: most of the questions we ask about cinema (how the arts combine, how space and time are narrated, how the spectator experiences emotion) were being asked about theater, painting, music and poetry centuries before cinema.

item.title: Week 5 · Day 1: What is film theory? Stam’s introduction and the “prehistory” of theory (part 1)
item.description: Film theory was not born from scratch along with cinema: it is the re-asking, in front of a new apparatus, of questions posed long before cinema — “what is an image, what is imitation, what does the spectator believe?”

item.title: Week 4 · Day 7: Test — Editing and sound
item.description: Editing and sound are two invisible hands that shape how the viewer constructs space, time and meaning; this week you learned to make those hands visible, and today we put that to the test.

item.title: Week 4 · Day 6: Film day — À bout de souffle and The Conversation
item.description: You will watch this week’s rules of editing and sound at work in two films: one deliberately breaks the rules of the image, the other turns sound into the story itself.

item.title: Week 4 · Day 5: Sound II — Sound in space and time
item.description: Where and when a sound exists in a film can be set independently of what the image tells us; filmmakers use this gap to create meaning, suspense and transitions.

item.title: Week 4 · Day 4: Sound I — The power of sound and its basic properties
item.description: Sound is not an “ornament” added behind the image; it is a formal element, as carefully chosen and edited as the image, that guides what we see, where we look and how we interpret what we see.

item.title: Week 4 · Day 3: Beyond continuity — editing time and breaking the rules
item.description: The continuity system is not a law of nature but a choice; editing can compress, stretch and scramble time, and by breaking the rules on purpose it can turn the viewer’s attention to the film itself.

item.title: Week 4 · Day 2: The continuity system — the 180° rule, eyeline match and shot/reverse shot
item.description: Continuity editing is a system developed to rebuild a fragmented space in the viewer’s mind as a single, coherent space — a system whose rules are deliberately learned, yet which we almost never notice while watching.

item.title: Week 4 · Day 1: What is editing? The four relations between shots
item.description: Editing is not simply joining one shot to the next; every cut creates a graphic, rhythmic, spatial and temporal relation between two shots, and the filmmaker consciously chooses each of these four relations.

item.title: Week 3 · Day 7: Exam — Mise-en-scène and cinematography
item.description: A shot’s meaning arises from two sets of decisions working together: what is placed in front of the camera (mise-en-scène) and how it is recorded (cinematography).

item.title: Week 3 · Day 6: Film day — Tokyo Story and the opening of Touch of Evil
item.description: The concepts of mise-en-scène and cinematography you read about this week become visible in two diametrically opposed styles: Ozu’s fixed, low, calm camera and Welles’s all-encompassing, restless one.

item.title: Week 3 · Day 5: Cinematography III — Mobile framing and the duration of the shot
item.description: When the camera moves and the shot lengthens, the frame stops being just a vantage point and becomes a narrator flowing through time: what we see, when, and in what order is now decided not by the cut but by the frame itself.

item.title: Week 3 · Day 4: Cinematography II — Framing: aspect ratio, offscreen space, angle, height and distance
item.description: The frame is not an empty window: by deciding what stays in, what is left out, and from what height, angle and distance our gaze arrives, it interprets the image for us before we ever see it.

item.title: Week 3 · Day 3: Cinematography I — Photographic qualities: tonality, speed, lens and focus
item.description: The camera does not record what is in front of it “as it is”; through the chosen tonality, speed, lens and focus, the same mise-en-scène becomes a completely different image, and therefore a completely different meaning.

item.title: Week 3 · Day 2: Mise-en-scène II — Lighting, staging, space and time
item.description: Mise-en-scène is not an inventory of objects but a system of guidance: lighting and staging organize where our gaze will go within the frame, and when.

item.title: Week 3 · Day 1: Mise-en-scène I — The concept, setting, costume and makeup
item.description: Mise-en-scène is everything placed in front of the camera; and a film chooses it not because it is “realistic” but because it does a job within the film as a whole.

item.title: Week 2 · Day 7: Quiz — Narrative
item.description: A film does not give us the story; it gives us the plot, and we build the story ourselves — every concept this week describes how that building work is guided.

item.title: Week 2 · Day 6: Film day — Rashomon (and, optionally, Memento)
item.description: Every narrative concept you learned this week actually names a piece of work the viewer does in their head; today you will do that work deliberately: you will try to build a story in your mind from what is shown on screen (the plot) and notice where that becomes difficult.

item.title: Week 2 · Day 5: Depth of Narration, Reliability and Diegesis
item.description: A film chooses not only how much information to give us (range) but also how far inside a character we will be when we receive it (depth); Rashomon shows that this second choice is never innocent.

item.title: Week 2 · Day 4: Range of Narration — Restricted and Unrestricted Narration
item.description: Every film doles out story information to the viewer in a particular measure: either it limits us to what a single character knows, or it shows us what none of the characters know; this choice determines whether a scene will produce curiosity, suspense or surprise.
